chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
title: Parker said it was practice
summary: Coleman tells of Bird's interview with Paul Desmond saying he practiced 14-18 hours a day.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: When I send you this other stuff, I’m going to send you this interview I have of Charlie Parker. I don’t think I gave it to you already.
I’ve never heard him speak at length. I couldn’t get hardly anything out of him.
I’ve got a couple interviews. I’ll send it to you.

One is an interview where Paul Desmond is interviewing him. It’s a good interview. Paul Desmond asks him, how did you get this incredible technique and all this stuff and everything, and Bird, he said, practice.

And then Paul Desmond starts laughing. He says, I’m glad you said that, because a lot of these young musicians out here, they think that you just are naturally like this and that you can just do this, it’s just genius. Bird said, oh no. He said, at one point I practiced 14 to 18 hours a day every day.

He said that it’s just like a good shoe, a fine shoe. When you polish it, it gets much better. He used that analogy. He said, anything can be polished up. He said, it’s not done with mirrors and tricks. He said, it’s just work.
I’m glad he said that too, because one time when I heard him play, I just figured, this man just picked the saxophone up and started playing it. But I guess, no.

Like you said, it could be 80% or 85% of whatever. There’s got to be a lot of talent there, but on top, there’s also – it’s true there’s a lot of people with talent that don’t – never fulfill their whole thing, because they don’t work.
